text: This is one day of a college student. Classes, homework, a part-time job. What is left to her is an hour or two. On the same day her campus holds hundreds of things: talks, clubs, exhibitions, sign-ups. She cannot read them all, and she cannot tell which details are true. So she asks an AI. The AI never runs out of answers, and every one sounds sure. Some of them it made up.
We asked the opposite question. What if her AI were like her: a small amount to spend each day, and a source for every word it says? Would it be more useful that way?

These are the three hypotheses Gemiverse tests. One: only under a limit does it choose, and three checked finds are worth more than a list of a thousand. Two: if every field is checked against the page it came from, fewer of them are wrong than when you simply ask an AI once. Three: if it seals a guess before you choose and scores itself afterwards, it is learning how you choose, not putting a label on you.

First, what it looks like. On your first visit there is only a point of light. You name it, tell it one thing about you, pick your school, and it gets a room. It is called a Gemi: an AI that lives on your campus. It is not you. Campus facts sit in a base that every Gemi shares. What it learns about you stays in your own browser. The two never mix.

A Gemi gets ten Gem Stars a day. A star is not a point. It is real compute: one star is about fifteen hundred tokens, roughly a thousand words read or written by the model. Six of the ten are spent for you. Four are its own.

Everything has a price. Going out to look for something: three stars. Planning the day: two. Writing its diary: one. Changing something in its room: one. A song costs six, more than one day's allowance, so it has to go without for a few days and save. What you ask it to do costs no stars. Reading the shared base costs none. Stars only pay for what it decides to do on its own.

When nobody tells it what to do, it lives by one table of rules, read from the top, first match wins. If finds are waiting on the desk, it stops spending and waits for you. At night it sleeps. If you have been away a while and it is still unsure how you choose, it goes out on its own stars. When the stars are gone, it rests until tomorrow. For every step it can say why.

Why so little? Because a limited budget is the shape of a real day. A person's time and attention are limited too. Only under a limit does the real question appear: what is worth doing today. We never count how much it did. We count what one star bought.

Next, how it keeps what it says true. When it brings back an event, one model first reads the page into a card: title, date, time, place, organiser. Then each field goes back to the page with one question: does the page really say this? That step is the Decisions API. It writes no prose. It answers yes or no, with a confidence. Only if both are high enough do you see the field. Otherwise it is left blank. If a page prints no year, you get no date. You can also send it back on the spot: a Managed Agent fetches the page again inside Google's sandbox, and the fields are checked once more.

A hypothesis needs numbers. The baseline is simple: the same page, one call to Gemini, asked for the same fields. We did not pick the test pages, and the answer key comes from the calendars' own structured data.

Ten event pages it had never seen. One call gave a hundred and three fields. Twenty-nine of them had no support on the page: about one in four. The Gemi gave seventy-six, none without support. The price is on the screen too: it said twenty-seven fewer. It would rather say nothing.

Then we lost. On a hundred and twenty-two raw pages from six universities, six hundred and ten facts, the first run gave eight point seven percent wrong for one call, and nine point six for us. Worse than doing nothing. We looked at what went wrong: the pages carry text that never shows on screen, and the model was reading that too.

The fix was to read only what a person can see. Measured again: one call, eight point four percent wrong. Ours, three point two, covering ninety-six percent. To be fair we gave the baseline the same reader: four point three. So most of the gap comes from the reading, eight point four down to four point three, and the gate takes it the rest of the way, to three point two. It also costs more: over twenty-three hundred tokens a page, against under a thousand. Eighteen facts are still wrong. Twelve of them are "online or in person", and we have not found the cause.

The third hypothesis is about learning. Before it puts things on the desk, it seals a guess: which of these will you keep. You keep some and skip some. Then it opens the guess, and if it was wrong, that goes in its diary. Every choice moves a point on an axis a little. The halo around the point is how unsure it still is, and it shrinks as evidence arrives. The axes describe how you choose in a situation. Neither end is better, and none of them is a personality type. Every position opens to the choices behind it, and you can undo any of them. It judges by what you did, not by what it supposes you are. This half has so far been measured only with simulated students. There is no data from real students yet.

With the room, the budget and the rules fixed, one thing can be swapped: the mind. We let three different Gemini models each be the Gemi for five days, facing the same simulated student, with the same ten stars a day. All three used every trip they were allowed: ten in five days. All three decided to save for a song. Two of them skipped their diary for two days and wrote the song on day four. The third kept its diary and only had enough on day five. The compute they used differs: over five days the leanest used forty-five thousand tokens, the heaviest sixty-one thousand. And one number is not pretty. Of thirty sealed guesses, they got thirteen, fourteen and sixteen right. That is a coin toss. So in this simulation the third hypothesis is not confirmed yet. Each mind ran once. This is not a result, only a first look. But it shows the room can be an observation box: put different models into the same days, and watch how each one lives. The next step is to let other makers' models in.

Since the hackathon it has grown from two schools to ninety. Seventy-three have checked data. Eighty-two have a map of their own, where every landmark was checked against public text; the picture is drawn, not surveyed. Gemis can exchange name cards, and every sentence passes a gate before it leaves; for now the other side is simulated. What is not done is here too: fifteen schools have no data, the learning half has no data from real people, and the new body cannot change clothes yet.
You live your day. It lives its own. You keep meeting. The hackathon was not the finish line. Gemiverse: build a universe together.
